display.purpose: The pick countdown only — the single loudest element on screen, visible across a room.

headline.purpose: On-the-clock team name and the Round · Pick readout flanking the countdown.

title.purpose: The draft name (h1) in the top chrome.

body.purpose: Search, list rows, banners, dialog copy, and form fields.

label.purpose: Uppercase broadcast supers — On the clock, On deck, Round · Pick, Recent picks.

shadows.name: floating-menu
shadows.purpose: The only shadow in the system — search dropdown, ⋯ overflow menu, Download menu. Reserved for layers that float over the board.

motion.name: colon-blink
motion.purpose: The countdown separator blinks like a broadcast clock.

motion.name: ticker-marquee
motion.purpose: Recent-picks marquee; only runs with ≥5 picks, pauses on hover, soft-fade edges.

motion.name: live-pulse
motion.purpose: The pulsing 'live' dot beside Recent picks.

motion.name: state-transition
motion.purpose: Default easing for button/border/fill state changes — color only, never layout.

motion.name: reduced-motion
motion.purpose: Colon, marquee, and live dot all fall back to static. Non-optional.

narrative.overview: Big Board is a stadium scoreboard that happens to run in a browser. When a league gathers in one room for its draft — board thrown up on a TV, everyone else following on a phone — the interface carries the charge of live sports broadcast: a giant countdown, a team spotlighted on the clock, a recent-picks ticker crawling along the bottom, a pulsing live dot. The identity is dark by default because the reference is a broadcast lower-third and a jumbotron in a dim room, not a document; a light theme exists and the scoreboard adapts with it — the --bb-* ramp flips to a warm beige sand card on a light page, with fills staying bright green and text/icon/ring greens, ambers, and reds darkening so they stay legible on the beige card. Density is deliberately low where it counts — 96px numerals, 52px team names, generous padding — while the draft grid underneath is the one place density is welcome, because it's a box score. The palette is a near-black blue-slate carrying a single electric green as the voice of go/live/your-turn, amber for caution, coral for over-time, and a functional position palette on the grid. It rejects two things: cuteness (no cartoon rounding, mascots, or emoji-as-UI) and the spreadsheet (no Bloomberg-terminal hairline density that rewards leaning in).
keyCharacteristics: Broadcast-first: the scoreboard is the hero; the countdown is the loudest element on screen.
Dark, near-black blue-slate surfaces with one electric-green accent for live/go/your-turn.
Position-as-color: QB/RB/WR/TE/DEF each own a hue so the grid reads as a heat map.
Space Grotesk throughout, tabular numerals everywhere numbers move.
Motion is status, not decoration: blinking colon, crawling ticker, pulsing live dot — all with reduced-motion fallbacks.
Two surfaces, one voice: a phone in the hand and a TV across the room are both primary.

rules.name: The Two-Stage Rule
rules.body: The app has two intentional surfaces: the broadcast stage (the scoreboard, on the dark --bb-* ramp) is the hero; the utility stage (the draft grid box score, the forms, the dialogs, on the slate ramp) is the workhorse. Keep them distinct — do not push --bb-* surfaces into the grid or dialogs. Only the accent green and the type system are shared across both stages.

rules.name: The One Green Rule
rules.body: The system has one accent green: Scoreboard Green (#3fe081). The action-emerald (#10b981) on the home/join/create surfaces is a legacy Tailwind default — treat every new green as Scoreboard Green and migrate old emerald toward it.

rules.name: The Functional-Color Rule
rules.body: Saturated color on the grid is never decoration — a hue means a position or a state. If a color isn't encoding position or state, it doesn't belong on the board.

rules.name: The Tabular Rule
rules.body: Anything that counts, ticks, or gets scanned column-against-column uses tabular-nums — the clock, overall pick numbers, round·pick, on-deck chips.

rules.name: The Flat-Signage Rule
rules.body: Resting surfaces are flat. Step the tonal ramp or add a 1px stroke instead of a shadow. Shadow is reserved for things that float over the board (menus, popovers).

rules.name: The State-By-Ring Rule
rules.body: Selection and status are shown with inset rings and background tints, never elevation: on-the-clock green ring + wash, fill-target amber ring, focus border-to-green.

dos: Do keep the two stages distinct (The Two-Stage Rule): the scoreboard on the dark --bb-* ramp is the broadcast hero; the draft grid, forms, and dialogs stay on the slate ramp. Only the accent green and type system cross the seam.
Do make the countdown the loudest thing on screen — never shrink the 96px clock or 52px team name to fit more chrome.

Do let the scoreboard adapt to light mode: every --bb-* token is defined in both :root (dark) and html.light. Keep fills bright (--bb-accent) and use --bb-accent-text / the light-mode amber and danger for anything drawn as text, an icon, or a ring so it stays legible on the beige card.
Do use tabular-nums on every number that moves or aligns.
Do encode position and state with color — green on-the-clock, amber skipped/paused, coral over-time, fuchsia traded, and the QB/RB/WR/TE/DEF hue set.
Do hold a 44px minimum touch target on icon controls and give every control default/hover/focus/disabled states.
Do keep motion as status and always ship the prefers-reduced-motion fallback.
Do twice-gate destructive actions (Reset lives behind the ⋯ menu and a confirm dialog).
donts: Don't go cute — no cartoon rounding, mascots, or emoji-as-UI; the lone football glyph in the wordmark is the ceiling.
Don't turn the board into a spreadsheet — no hairline density or sub-10px type outside the grid cells.
Don't introduce a third green or add new UI in action-emerald — converge on Scoreboard Green (#3fe081).
Don't use shadow to separate resting surfaces; step the tonal ramp or add a 1px stroke.
Don't use a colored border-left/border-right stripe as an accent; use full borders, tints, or rings.
Don't use gradient text or background-clip: text; emphasis comes from weight, size, and the one green.
Don't let a long team or player name overflow its cell or the on-the-clock slot — test real roster names at phone width.
Don't lean on glassmorphism; the one backdrop-blur (theme toggle) is the exception.
